name: carbon_leakage_net_effect
description: Condition under which a national carbon price produces a negative net effect on the consumption-based footprint of a tradable product: the shift term must exceed the abatement term. Includes the general formula, the tipping point, and five worked examples (tomatoes CH/DE, steel-like).

words.name: consumption-based footprint
words.description: greenhouse gas emissions attributed to domestic consumption of a product, regardless of production location; contrast with the territorial (UNFCCC production-based) inventory

words.name: abatement term
words.description: emission change from reduced domestic production intensity, applied to the initial domestic share: (1 - m0) * (eA - e0); non-positive

words.name: shift term
words.description: emission change from production relocating to the foreign producer: (m - m0) * (eB - eA); non-negative when the foreign producer is dirtier

words.name: leakage rate
words.description: L = foreign emission increase divided by domestic emission decrease; the net effect is negative exactly when L exceeds 100 percent

words.name: tipping import increase
words.description: critical increase of the import share dm* above which the net effect turns negative: dm* = (1 - m0) * (e0 - eA) / (eB - eA)

words.name: e0
words.description: domestic emission intensity before the carbon price change, in kg CO2eq per kg product (tomato examples) or t CO2eq per t product (steel example)

words.name: eA
words.description: domestic emission intensity after abatement triggered by the carbon price

words.name: eB
words.description: emission intensity of the imported product including transport

words.name: m0
words.description: import share of domestic consumption before the carbon price change, dimensionless fraction

words.name: m
words.description: import share of domestic consumption after the carbon price change, dimensionless fraction

formulas.name: net effect per unit of consumption
formulas.description: change of the consumption-based footprint per kg of product at constant consumption; first summand is the abatement term, second is the shift term

formulas.name: negative net effect condition
formulas.description: the net effect is negative if and only if the shift term exceeds the absolute abatement term; abatement therefore does not need to be zero, only smaller than the shift

formulas.name: necessary condition invariance
formulas.description: at full import the abatement intensity eA cancels; a negative net effect is possible for some m <= 1 if and only if eB > e0, independent of how much abatement occurs

values.context: oil-heated winter greenhouse tomatoes, Germany, including road transport to Switzerland
values.note: literature range for heated greenhouse tomatoes is roughly 2 to 6 kg CO2eq per kg; 6 is an upper-range illustration, to be replaced by a verified LCA value

values.context: heat-pump greenhouse tomatoes on Swiss hydro electricity, remaining emissions from cultivation, substrate, fertiliser, packaging
steel, EU average blast-furnace route before additional carbon pricing
values.unit: t CO2eq per t crude steel
values.note: order of magnitude consistent with IEA and worldsteel figures; verify against a specific dataset before citing

values.context: steel, coal-based blast-furnace route with coal-heavy electricity mix, typical for imports from China
values.unit: t CO2eq per t crude steel
values.note: verify against IEA or CBAM default values before citing

examples.name: abatement dominates
examples.note: carbon price triggers a switch from oil heating to heat pump; import share rises only moderately; footprint falls by two thirds

examples.name: tipping point with partial abatement
examples.note: with abatement from 3 to 1 the tipping point is an import-share increase of 36 percentage points, i.e. m = 0.46

examples.name: shift dominates despite abatement
examples.note: domestic intensity falls by two thirds, yet the consumption footprint rises by two thirds because the shift term 0.8 * 5 exceeds the abatement term 0.9 * 2; demonstrates that zero abatement is not required for a negative net effect

examples.name: both effects, abatement wins
examples.note: 60 percent leakage and still a positive net effect; leakage below 100 percent weakens but does not reverse the measure

examples.name: steel-like moderate intensity ratio
examples.note: even at an intensity ratio of only 1.5 the net effect turns slightly negative once the import share rises from 20 to 50 percent; the tipping increase is 23 percentage points

assumptions: consumption volume is constant; a demand response to higher prices would reduce total emissions and shift all tipping points upward
eB is constant, i.e. the foreign producer does not abate; a foreign carbon price would lower eB and can remove the negative-net-effect region entirely
the fossil world-market channel (lower domestic fossil demand lowering world prices and raising consumption elsewhere) is excluded; it can only worsen the balance
single product, two countries; the import-share response m(carbon price differential) is treated as an input, not modelled

conclusions.statement: a negative net effect requires the shift term to exceed the abatement term, not the absence of abatement
the necessary condition eB > e0 is invariant to the amount of domestic abatement; abatement only raises the tipping import increase dm_star
net effect negative is equivalent to leakage rate above 100 percent

a bilateral border carbon adjustment priced at the carbon-price differential times the verified product intensity neutralises the shift term; the only missing input in practice is a verifiable eB per product and origin

sources.name: parameter values
sources.description: all numeric parameters are illustrative and tagged as assumed values; before publication replace tomato intensities with a verified LCA source and steel intensities with IEA, worldsteel or EU CBAM default values
